# libvips selects a loader from a file's actual bytes, not from its declared content type. These
# tests pin which loader is selected for each file type under the app's configured loader policy
# (config/initializers/vips.rb).
class VipsLoaderPolicyTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  # Header bytes are enough for libvips to identify a format; native types are encoded live, exotic
  # ones are represented by their magic bytes.
  FTYP_AVIF = "\x00\x00\x00\x1cftypavif\x00\x00\x00\x00avifmif1miaf".b
  FTYP_HEIC = "\x00\x00\x00\x1cftypheic\x00\x00\x00\x00heicmif1miaf".b
  BMP = "BM" + [ 0, 0, 54 ].pack("V3") + "\x00" * 40
  PSD = "8BPS" + [ 1 ].pack("n") + "\x00" * 26
  ICO = "\x00\x00\x01\x00\x01\x00" + "\x00" * 16
  SVG = %q(<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="8" height="8"/>)

  test "loads PNG" do
    assert_equal "VipsForeignLoadPngFile", loader_for(encode("png"))
  end

  test "loads GIF" do
    assert_equal "VipsForeignLoadNsgifFile", loader_for(encode("gif"))
  end

  test "loads JPEG" do
    assert_equal "VipsForeignLoadJpegFile", loader_for(encode("jpg"))
  end

  test "loads TIFF" do
    assert_equal "VipsForeignLoadTiffFile", loader_for(encode("tif"))
  end

  test "loads WebP" do
    assert_equal "VipsForeignLoadWebpFile", loader_for(encode("webp"))
  end

  test "loads AVIF" do
    assert_equal "VipsForeignLoadHeifFile", loader_for(FTYP_AVIF)
  end

  test "loads HEIC" do
    assert_equal "VipsForeignLoadHeifFile", loader_for(FTYP_HEIC)
  end

  test "denies BMP through magickload" do
    assert_nil loader_for(BMP)
  end

  test "denies PSD through magickload" do
    assert_nil loader_for(PSD)
  end

  test "denies ICO through magickload" do
    assert_nil loader_for(ICO)
  end

  test "denies SVG through svgload" do
    assert_nil loader_for(SVG)
  end

  test "denies OpenSlide files through openslideload" do
    # OpenSlide files can segfault the embedded sqlite in forked parallel workers
    assert_loader_blocked :openslideload, ".svs"
  end

  test "denies FITS files through fitsload" do
    assert_loader_blocked :fitsload, ".fits"
  end

  test "denies MATLAB files through matload" do
    assert_loader_blocked :matload, ".mat"
  end

  test "denies NIFTI files through niftiload" do
    assert_loader_blocked :niftiload, ".nii"
  end

  test "denies RAW files through dcrawload" do
    assert_loader_blocked :dcrawload, ".raw"
  end

  test "denies VIPS files through vipsload" do
    assert_loader_blocked :vipsload, ".vips"
  end

  private
    # Invoke a specific libvips loader directly and assert it is refused because the
    # operation is blocked (rather than because the bytes are not a valid image).
    def assert_loader_blocked(operation, extension)
      Tempfile.create([ "blocked_loader", extension ], binmode: true) do |file|
        file.write "not an image"
        file.flush

        error = assert_raises(Vips::Error) { Vips::Image.public_send(operation, file.path) }
        actual = error.message.chomp

        # note that exception message may include multiple errors on separate lines,
        # so `^` and `$` anchors are used instead of `\A` and `\z`.
        if actual =~ /^VipsOperation: class \"#{operation}\" not found$/
          skip "libvips does not support #{operation} on this system"
        end
        assert_match(/^#{operation}: operation is blocked$/, actual)
      end
    end

    def encode(ext)
      Vips::Image.black(8, 8).add(128).cast("uchar").write_to_buffer(".#{ext}")
    end

    def loader_for(bytes)
      Tempfile.create(%w[loader_probe .img], binmode: true) do |file|
        file.write bytes
        file.flush
        Vips.vips_foreign_find_load(file.path)
      end
    end
end
"
}

# Style

We aim to write code that is a pleasure to read, and we have a lot of opinions about how to do it well. Writing great code is an essential part of our programming culture, and we deliberately set a high bar for every code change anyone contributes. We care about how code reads, how code looks, and how code makes you feel when you read it.

We love discussing code. If you have questions about how to write something, or if you detect some smell you are not quite sure how to solve, please ask away to other programmers. A Pull Request is a great way to do this.

When writing new code, unless you are very familiar with our approach, try to find similar code elsewhere to look for inspiration.

## Conditional returns

In general, we prefer to use expanded conditionals over guard clauses.

```ruby
# Bad
def todos_for_new_group
  ids = params.require(:todolist)[:todo_ids]
  return [] unless ids
  @bucket.recordings.todos.find(ids.split(","))
end

# Good
def todos_for_new_group
  if ids = params.require(:todolist)[:todo_ids]
    @bucket.recordings.todos.find(ids.split(","))
  else
    []
  end
end
```

This is because guard clauses can be hard to read, especially when they are nested.

As an exception, we sometimes use guard clauses to return early from a method:

* When the return is right at the beginning of the method.
* When the main method body is not trivial and involves several lines of code.

```ruby
def after_recorded_as_commit(recording)
  return if recording.parent.was_created?

  if recording.was_created?
    broadcast_new_column(recording)
  else
    broadcast_column_change(recording)
  end
end
```

## Methods ordering

We order methods in classes in the following order:

1. `class` methods
2. `public` methods with `initialize` at the top.
3. `private` methods

## Invocation order

We order methods vertically based on their invocation order. This helps us to understand the flow of the code.

```ruby
class SomeClass
  def some_method
    method_1
    method_2
  end

  private
    def method_1
      method_1_1
      method_1_2
    end
  
    def method_1_1
      # ...
    end
  
    def method_1_2
      # ...
    end
  
    def method_2
      method_2_1
      method_2_2
    end
  
    def method_2_1
      # ...
    end
  
    def method_2_2
      # ...
    end
end
```

## To bang or not to bang

Should I call a method `do_something` or `do_something!`?

As a general rule, we only use `!` for methods that have a correspondent counterpart without `!`. In particular, we don’t use `!` to flag destructive actions. There are plenty of destructive methods in Ruby and Rails that do not end with `!`.

## Visibility modifiers

We don't add a newline under visibility modifiers, and we indent the content under them.

```ruby
class SomeClass
  def some_method
    # ...
  end

  private
    def some_private_method_1
      # ...
    end

    def some_private_method_2
      # ...
    end
end
```

If a module only has private methods, we mark it `private` at the top and add an extra new line after but don't indent.

```ruby
module SomeModule
  private
  
  def some_private_method
    # ...
  end
end
```

## CRUD controllers

We model web endpoints as CRUD operations on resources (REST). When an action doesn't map cleanly to a standard CRUD verb, we introduce a new resource rather than adding custom actions.

```ruby
# Bad
resources :cards do
  post :close
  post :reopen
end

# Good
resources :cards do
  resource :closure
end
```

## Controller and model interactions

In general, we favor a [vanilla Rails](https://dev.37signals.com/vanilla-rails-is-plenty/) approach with thin controllers directly invoking a rich domain model. We don't use services or other artifacts to connect the two.

Invoking plain Active Record operations is totally fine:

```ruby
class Cards::CommentsController < ApplicationController
  def create
    @comment = @card.comments.create!(comment_params)
  end
end
```

For more complex behavior, we prefer clear, intention-revealing model APIs that controllers call directly:

```ruby
class Cards::GoldnessesController < ApplicationController
  def create
    @card.gild
  end
end
```

When justified, it is fine to use services or form objects, but don't treat those as special artifacts:

```ruby
Signup.new(email_address: email_address).create_identity
```

## Run async operations in jobs

As a general rule, we write shallow job classes that delegate the logic itself to domain models:

* We typically use the suffix `_later` to flag methods that enqueue a job.
* A common scenario is having a model class that enqueues a job that, when executed, invokes some method in that same class. In this case, we use the suffix `_now` for the regular synchronous method.

```ruby
module Event::Relaying
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    after_create_commit :relay_later
  end

  def relay_later
    Event::RelayJob.perform_later(self)
  end

  def relay_now
    # ...
  end
end

class Event::RelayJob < ApplicationJob
  def perform(event)
    event.relay_now
  end
end
```

* When the main method body is not trivial and involves several lines of code.

```ruby
def after_recorded_as_commit(recording)
  return if recording.parent.was_created?

  if recording.was_created?
    broadcast_new_column(recording)
  else
    broadcast_column_change(recording)
  end
end
```

## Methods ordering

We order methods in classes in the following order:

1. `class` methods
2. `public` methods with `initialize` at the top.
3. `private` methods

## Invocation order

We order methods vertically based on their invocation order. This helps us to understand the flow of the code.

```ruby
class SomeClass
  def some_method
    method_1
    method_2
  end

  private
    def method_1
      method_1_1
      method_1_2
    end
  
    def method_1_1
      # ...
    end
  
    def method_1_2
      # ...
    end
  
    def method_2
      method_2_1
      method_2_2
    end
  
    def method_2_1
      # ...
    end
  
    def method_2_2
      # ...
    end
end
```

## To bang or not to bang

Should I call a method `do_something` or `do_something!`?

As a general rule, we only use `!` for methods that have a correspondent counterpart without `!`. In particular, we don’t use `!` to flag destructive actions. There are plenty of destructive methods in Ruby and Rails that do not end with `!`.

## Visibility modifiers

We don't add a newline under visibility modifiers, and we indent the content under them.

```ruby
class SomeClass
  def some_method
    # ...
  end

  private
    def some_private_method_1
      # ...
    end

    def some_private_method_2
      # ...
    end
end
```

If a module only has private methods, we mark it `private` at the top and add an extra new line after but don't indent.

```ruby
module SomeModule
  private
  
  def some_private_method
    # ...
  end
end
```

## CRUD controllers

We model web endpoints as CRUD operations on resources (REST). When an action doesn't map cleanly to a standard CRUD verb, we introduce a new resource rather than adding custom actions.

```ruby
# Bad
resources :cards do
  post :close
  post :reopen
end

# Good
resources :cards do
  resource :closure
end
```

## Controller and model interactions

In general, we favor a [vanilla Rails](https://dev.37signals.com/vanilla-rails-is-plenty/) approach with thin controllers directly invoking a rich domain model. We don't use services or other artifacts to connect the two.

Invoking plain Active Record operations is totally fine:

```ruby
class Cards::CommentsController < ApplicationController
  def create
    @comment = @card.comments.create!(comment_params)
  end
end
```

For more complex behavior, we prefer clear, intention-revealing model APIs that controllers call directly:

```ruby
class Cards::GoldnessesController < ApplicationController
  def create
    @card.gild
  end
end
```

When justified, it is fine to use services or form objects, but don't treat those as special artifacts:

```ruby
Signup.new(email_address: email_address).create_identity
```

## Run async operations in jobs

As a general rule, we write shallow job classes that delegate the logic itself to domain models:

* We typically use the suffix `_later` to flag methods that enqueue a job.
* A common scenario is having a model class that enqueues a job that, when executed, invokes some method in that same class. In this case, we use the suffix `_now` for the regular synchronous method.

```ruby
module Event::Relaying
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    after_create_commit :relay_later
  end

  def relay_later
    Event::RelayJob.perform_later(self)
  end

  def relay_now
    # ...
  end
end

class Event::RelayJob < ApplicationJob
  def perform(event)
    event.relay_now
  end
end
```

Even in production, the `saas/config/environments/production.rb` is run before the default and sets the mailer configurations. The SaaS configurations remain completely untouched even if deployed to a production environment. Good.

Second, let's anticipate user mistakes with the `APP_HOST`. Humans are bound to make typos or copy-paste errors. I'm thinking of someone accidentally putting "https://" or a trailing slash in `APP_HOST`. If the user does it, then the Rails' `url_for` can generate broken URLs. But if we normalize the `APP_HOST` value to strip those things, it's foolproof. Removes the potential for broken URLs, and simplifies configuration. A developer could copy paste `my-fizzy.com` in their browser and not have to think about editing it. Easy.

Third, what about a mismatch between `servers: web:` and `proxy: host:` in `config/deploy.yml` with `APP_HOST`? Is there a scenario where someone could edit server names, proxy hosts, mailer addresses, and forget to update the `APP_HOST`? That's a real concern. I'm re-thinking through scenarios:
*   **Scenario A**: Developer finds and replaces `fizzy.example.com` with `their-host`, updating all instances properly. `APP_HOST` gets updated. Good.
*   **Scenario B**: Developer puts `their-host` into `servers` and `proxy`. This also updates `APP_HOST`. Good.
*   **Scenario C**: A careless developer or an automated test changes `servers` and `proxy` but leaves `APP_HOST` as `fizzy.example.com`. That's bad.

However, `fizzy.example.com` is an example domain. It can NEVER receive traffic or an SSL cert because *no one* can own it. It's reserved for documentation. Now, even if our tests are written with example domains, the problem isn't catastrophic, but it could introduce confusing false positives. I could write a test for it, but why add more magic? Then I'm thinking even better, is there a way to eliminate any chance of a mismatch? It *is* possible! By keeping the YAML file *without* aliases. We can make sure any tool can parse it. require "test_helper"
require "kamal"
require "open3"

class KamalDeployConfigTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  TEST_SECRETS = {
    "SECRET_KEY_BASE" => "0" * 64,
    "VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY" => "public-key",
    "VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY" => "private-key",
    "SMTP_USERNAME" => "smtp-user",
    "SMTP_PASSWORD" => "smtp-password"
  }.freeze

  test "one-box kamal config is valid and configures proxy SSL, SQLite storage volume, jobs in Puma, mail, and secrets" do
    with_env(TEST_SECRETS) do
      config = Kamal::Configuration.create_from(config_file: Rails.root.join("config/deploy.yml"))
      web_role = config.role(:web)

      assert_equal "fizzy", config.service
      assert_equal [ "web" ], config.roles.map(&:name)
      assert_empty config.accessories

      assert web_role.ssl?
      assert_equal [ "fizzy.example.com" ], web_role.proxy.hosts

      assert config.registry.local?
      assert_includes config.volume_args, "fizzy_storage:/rails/storage"
      assert_equal "/rails/public/assets", web_role.asset_path

      assert_equal true, config.env.clear["SOLID_QUEUE_IN_PUMA"]
      assert_equal "fizzy.example.com", config.env.clear["APP_HOST"]
      assert_equal "smtp.example.com", config.env.clear["SMTP_ADDRESS"]
      assert_equal 587, config.env.clear["SMTP_PORT"]
      assert config.env.clear["MAILER_FROM_ADDRESS"].present?

      TEST_SECRETS.each_key do |secret_key|
        assert_includes config.env.secret_keys, secret_key
      end
    end
  end

  test "production environment configures HTTPS URL options and SMTP from environment variables" do
    env = TEST_SECRETS.merge(
      "RAILS_ENV" => "production",
      "SAAS" => "false",
      "BUNDLE_GEMFILE" => Rails.root.join("Gemfile").to_s,
      "APP_HOST" => "https://fizzy.their-host.example/",
      "SMTP_ADDRESS" => "mail.their-host.example",
      "SMTP_PORT" => "2525"
    )

    script = <<~RUBY
      puts({
        controller_url: Rails.application.config.action_controller.default_url_options,
        mailer_url: Rails.application.config.action_mailer.default_url_options,
        routes_url: Rails.application.routes.default_url_options,
        smtp: ActionMailer::Base.smtp_settings
      }.to_json)
    RUBY

    stdout, stderr, status = Open3.capture3(env, RbConfig.ruby, "bin/rails", "runner", script, chdir: Rails.root.to_s)
    assert status.success?, "Expected production runner to succeed, got:\n#{stderr}\n#{stdout}"

    result = JSON.parse(stdout.lines.last, symbolize_names: true)

    expected_url_options = { host: "fizzy.their-host.example", protocol: "https" }
    assert_equal expected_url_options, result[:controller_url]
    assert_equal expected_url_options, result[:mailer_url]
    assert_equal expected_url_options, result[:routes_url]

    assert_equal "mail.their-host.example", result[:smtp][:address]
    assert_equal 2525, result[:smtp][:port]
    assert_equal "fizzy.their-host.example", result[:smtp][:domain]
    assert_equal "smtp-user", result[:smtp][:user_name]
    assert_equal "smtp-password", result[:smtp][:password]
    assert_equal true, result[:smtp][:enable_starttls_auto]
  end

  test "production environment supports SMTPS (SMTP_TLS=true) and blank credentials without Mail::SMTP conflicts" do
    env = {
      "RAILS_ENV" => "production",
      "SAAS" => "false",
      "BUNDLE_GEMFILE" => Rails.root.join("Gemfile").to_s,
      "SECRET_KEY_BASE" => "0" * 64,
      "KAMAL_HOST" => "fizzy.kamal-host.example",
      "APP_HOST" => "",
      "SMTP_ADDRESS" => "smtps.their-host.example",
      "SMTP_PORT" => "465",
      "SMTP_TLS" => "true",
      "SMTP_USERNAME" => "",
      "SMTP_PASSWORD" => ""
    }

    script = <<~RUBY
      # Ensure Mail::SMTP accepts the settings without raising mutual-exclusivity ArgumentError
      Mail::SMTP.new(ActionMailer::Base.smtp_settings).send(:build_smtp_session)
      puts({
        mailer_url: Rails.application.config.action_mailer.default_url_options,
        smtp: ActionMailer::Base.smtp_settings
      }.to_json)
    RUBY

    stdout, stderr, status = Open3.capture3(env, RbConfig.ruby, "bin/rails", "runner", script, chdir: Rails.root.to_s)
    assert status.success?, "Expected SMTPS runner to succeed, got:\n#{stderr}\n#{stdout}"

    result = JSON.parse(stdout.lines.last, symbolize_names: true)
    assert_equal({ host: "fizzy.kamal-host.example", protocol: "https" }, result[:mailer_url])
    assert_equal true, result[:smtp][:tls]
    assert_equal false, result[:smtp][:enable_starttls_auto]
    assert_nil result[:smtp][:user_name]
    assert_nil result[:smtp][:password]
  end

  private
    def with_env(overrides)
      previous = overrides.keys.index_with { |key| ENV[key] }
      overrides.each { |key, value| ENV[key] = value }
      yield
    ensure
      previous.each do |key, value|
        if value.nil?
          ENV.delete(key)
        else
          ENV[key] = value
        end
      end
    end
end

require "test_helper"
require "kamal"
require "open3"

class KamalDeployConfigTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  TEST_SECRETS = {
    "SECRET_KEY_BASE" => "0" * 64,
    "VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY" => "public-key",
    "VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY" => "private-key",
    "SMTP_USERNAME" => "smtp-user",
    "SMTP_PASSWORD" => "smtp-password"
  }.freeze

  test "one-box kamal config is valid and configures proxy SSL, SQLite storage volume, jobs in Puma, mail, and secrets" do
    with_env(TEST_SECRETS) do
      config = Kamal::Configuration.create_from(config_file: Rails.root.join("config/deploy.yml"))
      web_role = config.role(:web)

      assert_equal "fizzy", config.service
      assert_equal [ "web" ], config.roles.map(&:name)
      assert_empty config.accessories

      assert web_role.ssl?
      assert_equal [ "fizzy.example.com" ], web_role.proxy.hosts

      assert config.registry.local?
      assert_includes config.volume_args, "fizzy_storage:/rails/storage"
      assert_equal "/rails/public/assets", web_role.asset_path

      assert_equal true, config.env.clear["SOLID_QUEUE_IN_PUMA"]
      assert_equal "fizzy.example.com", config.env.clear["APP_HOST"]
      assert_equal "smtp.example.com", config.env.clear["SMTP_ADDRESS"]
      assert_equal 587, config.env.clear["SMTP_PORT"]
      assert config.env.clear["MAILER_FROM_ADDRESS"].present?

      TEST_SECRETS.each_key do |secret_key|
        assert_includes config.env.secret_keys, secret_key
      end
    end
  end

  test "production environment configures HTTPS URL options and SMTP from environment variables" do
    env = TEST_SECRETS.merge(
      "RAILS_ENV" => "production",
      "SAAS" => "false",
      "BUNDLE_GEMFILE" => Rails.root.join("Gemfile").to_s,
      "APP_HOST" => "https://fizzy.their-host.example/",
      "SMTP_ADDRESS" => "mail.their-host.example",
      "SMTP_PORT" => "2525"
    )

    script = <<~RUBY
      puts({
        controller_url: Rails.application.config.action_controller.default_url_options,
        mailer_url: Rails.application.config.action_mailer.default_url_options,
        routes_url: Rails.application.routes.default_url_options,
        smtp: ActionMailer::Base.smtp_settings
      }.to_json)
    RUBY

    stdout, stderr, status = Open3.capture3(env, RbConfig.ruby, "bin/rails", "runner", script, chdir: Rails.root.to_s)
    assert status.success?, "Expected production runner to succeed, got:\n#{stderr}\n#{stdout}"

    result = JSON.parse(stdout.lines.last, symbolize_names: true)

    expected_url_options = { host: "fizzy.their-host.example", protocol: "https" }
    assert_equal expected_url_options, result[:controller_url]
    assert_equal expected_url_options, result[:mailer_url]
    assert_equal expected_url_options, result[:routes_url]

    assert_equal "mail.their-host.example", result[:smtp][:address]
    assert_equal 2525, result[:smtp][:port]
    assert_equal "fizzy.their-host.example", result[:smtp][:domain]
    assert_equal "smtp-user", result[:smtp][:user_name]
    assert_equal "smtp-password", result[:smtp][:password]
    assert_equal true, result[:smtp][:enable_starttls_auto]
  end

  test "production environment supports SMTPS (SMTP_TLS=true) and blank credentials without Mail::SMTP conflicts" do
    env = {
      "RAILS_ENV" => "production",
      "SAAS" => "false",
      "BUNDLE_GEMFILE" => Rails.root.join("Gemfile").to_s,
      "SECRET_KEY_BASE" => "0" * 64,
      "KAMAL_HOST" => "fizzy.kamal-host.example",
      "APP_HOST" => "",
      "SMTP_ADDRESS" => "smtps.their-host.example",
      "SMTP_PORT" => "465",
      "SMTP_TLS" => "true",
      "SMTP_USERNAME" => "",
      "SMTP_PASSWORD" => ""
    }

    script = <<~RUBY
      # Ensure Mail::SMTP accepts the settings without raising mutual-exclusivity ArgumentError
      Mail::SMTP.new(ActionMailer::Base.smtp_settings).send(:build_smtp_session)
      puts({
        mailer_url: Rails.application.config.action_mailer.default_url_options,
        smtp: ActionMailer::Base.smtp_settings
      }.to_json)
    RUBY

    stdout, stderr, status = Open3.capture3(env, RbConfig.ruby, "bin/rails", "runner", script, chdir: Rails.root.to_s)
    assert status.success?, "Expected SMTPS runner to succeed, got:\n#{stderr}\n#{stdout}"

    result = JSON.parse(stdout.lines.last, symbolize_names: true)
    assert_equal({ host: "fizzy.kamal-host.example", protocol: "https" }, result[:mailer_url])
    assert_equal true, result[:smtp][:tls]
    assert_equal false, result[:smtp][:enable_starttls_auto]
    assert_nil result[:smtp][:user_name]
    assert_nil result[:smtp][:password]
  end

  private
    def with_env(overrides)
      previous = overrides.keys.index_with { |key| ENV[key] }
      overrides.each { |key, value| ENV[key] = value }
      yield
    ensure
      previous.each do |key, value|
        if value.nil?
          ENV.delete(key)
        else
          ENV[key] = value
        end
      end
    end
end

I have added a single-server Kamal deployment configuration for Fizzy along with the corresponding production host and SMTP configuration:

- **`config/deploy.yml` & `.kamal/secrets`**:
  - Configures a single `web` container (`service: fizzy`, `image: fizzy`) using Kamal's SSH-forwarded local registry (`localhost:5555`) by default so no external container registry account is needed.
  - Enables automatic Let's Encrypt HTTPS termination on `kamal-proxy` (`proxy: { ssl: true, host: ... }`).
  - Mounts a persistent Docker volume (`fizzy_storage:/rails/storage`) so all SQLite databases (`production`, `cable`, `cache`, `queue`) and local Active Storage uploads survive subsequent deploys, and bridges `/rails/public/assets` across deploys.
  - Runs Solid Queue inside Puma (`SOLID_QUEUE_IN_PUMA: true`) so background jobs run inside the single container on the server.
  - Wires `APP_HOST`, `MAILER_FROM_ADDRESS`, `SMTP_ADDRESS`, and `SMTP_PORT` in `env.clear`, and `SECRET_KEY_BASE`, `VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY`, `VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY`, `SMTP_USERNAME`, and `SMTP_PASSWORD` via `.kamal/secrets`.
- **`config/environments/production.rb`**:
  - Configures `default_url_options` (on controllers, mailers, and routes) from `APP_HOST` (falling back to `APP_FQDN` / `KAMAL_HOST`) and `smtp_settings` from `SMTP_*` environment variables when not already set (preserving `fizzy-saas` configuration).
- **`.dockerignore`, `docs/deployment.md`, `README.md`, and `test/lib/kamal_deploy_config_test.rb`**:
  - Excludes `/config/deploy*.yml` and `/.kamal` from the Docker build context, documents the one-box Kamal setup workflow, and adds automated tests covering the Kamal config and production URL/SMTP settings.
